ipw, WeightIt and PSweight side by side

Source: vignettes/articles/ipw-and-weightit.Rmd
ipw-and-weightit.Rmd
library(ipw)
library(survival)

WeightIt (Greifer) and ipw both estimate weights for marginal structural models; PSweight (Zhou, Tong, Li, Thomas & Li) estimates propensity score weighted treatment effects for point treatments. This article runs the packages on the same data: a binary and a categorical point treatment, where all three apply and should give the same answer, and longitudinal data with individual visit times, where ipw and WeightIt work differently. WeightIt and PSweight are used only through their exported functions. This page was built with ipw 1.3.2.9000, WeightIt 2.1.0 and PSweight 2.1.2.

What PSweight offers. PSweight is designed for point treatments, binary or with several levels. It offers inverse probability, ATT, overlap, matching and entropy weights, propensity score trimming, and augmented (doubly robust) estimators that add an outcome model. The propensity score can be fitted by logistic or multinomial regression, generalized boosted models or SuperLearner. Inference uses sandwich (M-estimation) variances that account for the estimated propensity score, or the bootstrap, for differences in means and, for binary or count outcomes, risk ratios and odds ratios. It also has functions for survey data with survey weights and for clustered data, both mainly for binary treatments, and covariate balance summaries and plots. It does not handle time-varying treatments.

1. Binary point treatment

A confounder l, a binary covariate x, a binary treatment a and an outcome y; the effect of a on y is 2 for everyone, so all estimands are 2 in truth.

set.seed(2026)
n <- 1000
d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n), x = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4))
d$a <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.3 + 0.8 * d$l + 0.5 * d$x))
d$y <- 2 * d$a + d$l + d$x + rnorm(n)
stopifnot(all.equal(sum(d$y), stored$data_check))   # same data as the bootstrap
estimands <- c("ATE", "ATT", "ATC", "ATO")

The weights

With a logistic model, both packages fit the same propensity score with glm() and apply the same formulas, so the weights should agree up to rounding:

w_ipw <- lapply(setNames(estimands, estimands), function(est)
  ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
           denominator = ~ l + x, data = d, estimand = est))
w_wit <- lapply(setNames(estimands, estimands), function(est)
  WeightIt::weightit(a ~ l + x, data = d, method = "glm", estimand = est))
sapply(estimands, function(est)
  c(max.abs.difference = max(abs(w_ipw[[est]]$ipw.weights - w_wit[[est]]$weights)),
    max.weight = max(w_ipw[[est]]$ipw.weights)))
#>                             ATE          ATT          ATC          ATO
#> max.abs.difference 1.065814e-14 2.220446e-15 8.881784e-15 2.220446e-16
#> max.weight         1.180340e+01 8.832774e+00 1.080340e+01 9.152786e-01

The largest difference is at the level of floating-point rounding. Stabilized ATE weights agree too: numerator = ~ 1 in ipw and stabilize = TRUE in WeightIt.

PSweight scales the weights to sum to 1 within each treatment group, which changes no weighted group mean or effect estimate, so the weights are compared after the same scaling. PSweight has no “ATC” option, but its ATT weights with the untreated as the “treated” group (trtgrp = "0") are the ATC weights.

psw_args <- list(ATE = list(weight = "IPW"), ATT = list(weight = "treated"),
                 ATC = list(weight = "treated", trtgrp = "0"),
                 ATO = list(weight = "overlap"))
norm_by_group <- function(w, g) w / ave(w, g, FUN = sum)
w_ipw_bin <- lapply(setNames(estimands, estimands),
  function(est) ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                         denominator = ~ l + x, data = d, estimand = est)$ipw.weights)
sapply(estimands, function(est) {
  ss <- do.call(PSweight::SumStat, c(list(ps.formula = a ~ l + x, data = d), psw_args[[est]]))
  max(abs(norm_by_group(w_ipw_bin[[est]], d$a) -
          norm_by_group(ss$ps.weights[[psw_args[[est]]$weight]], d$a)))
})
#>          ATE          ATT          ATC          ATO 
#> 1.734723e-18 4.336809e-19 0.000000e+00 1.734723e-18

Standard errors

The marginal structural model is the weighted regression of y on a. Five standard errors of the coefficient of a:

  • ipwvcov(): ipw’s M-estimation standard error (new), which accounts for the estimation of the weights;
  • glm_weightit(vcov = “asympt”): WeightIt’s M-estimation standard error;
  • PSweight: the sandwich standard error of the weighted difference in means from PSweight() and summary(), which for the saturated model y ~ a is the same quantity;
  • robust (HC0): the sandwich standard error that treats the weights as known, as svyglm() or glm_weightit(vcov = "HC0") give it;
  • bootstrap: 2000 bootstrap samples, re-estimating the weights in each (computed once, see the setup chunk).
se_table <- t(sapply(estimands, function(est) {
  msm <- lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = w_ipw[[est]]$ipw.weights)
  fit_m <- WeightIt::glm_weightit(y ~ a, data = d, weightit = w_wit[[est]], vcov = "asympt")
  fit_r <- WeightIt::glm_weightit(y ~ a, data = d, weightit = w_wit[[est]], vcov = "HC0")
  c(estimate = unname(coef(msm)["a"]),
    ipwvcov = sqrt(ipwvcov(w_ipw[[est]], msm)["a", "a"]),
    glm_weightit.asympt = sqrt(vcov(fit_m)["a", "a"]),
    PSweight = if (has_psweight) unname(summary(do.call(PSweight::PSweight,
      c(list(ps.formula = a ~ l + x, yname = "y", data = d), psw_args[[est]])))$estimates[1, "Std.Error"])
      else NA,
    robust.HC0 = sqrt(vcov(fit_r)["a", "a"]),
    bootstrap = unname(stored$boot_se[est]))
}))
round(se_table, 4)
#>     estimate ipwvcov glm_weightit.asympt PSweight robust.HC0 bootstrap
#> ATE   2.0259  0.0804              0.0804   0.0804     0.1234    0.0836
#> ATT   2.1543  0.0862              0.0862   0.0862     0.1134    0.0878
#> ATC   1.9160  0.1094              0.1094   0.1094     0.1380    0.1131
#> ATO   2.0807  0.0684              0.0684   0.0684     0.0962    0.0703

ipwvcov(), glm_weightit(vcov = "asympt") and PSweight agree to many decimals: they solve the same stacked estimating equations (Lunceford & Davidian 2004), and in the package tests they agree to about 1e-9 or better. All three are close to the bootstrap. The robust standard error, which ignores that the weights were estimated, is larger for all four estimands here, so confidence intervals based on it would be wider than needed. For the ATE this is the usual direction (estimating the weights reduces the variance); for the ATT, ATC and ATO the robust standard error is not guaranteed to be conservative and can also be too small. The M-estimation or bootstrap standard error is therefore preferred.

A Cox outcome model

For a time-to-event outcome the MSM is a weighted Cox model. We add a survival time to the same data (hazard ratio exp(-0.5) for a, administrative censoring at 5) and compare ipwvcov() with coxph()’s robust standard error, which treats the weights as known, and with coxph_weightit(vcov = "asympt"):

set.seed(8)
t_ev <- rexp(nrow(d), 0.2 * exp(-0.5 * d$a + 0.5 * d$l + 0.3 * d$x))
d$status <- as.numeric(t_ev < 5)
d$time <- pmin(t_ev, 5)
cox_table <- t(sapply(estimands, function(est) {
  msm <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ a, data = d, weights = w_ipw[[est]]$ipw.weights)
  fit_w <- WeightIt::coxph_weightit(Surv(time, status) ~ a, data = d,
                                    weightit = w_wit[[est]], vcov = "asympt")
  c(log.hr = unname(coef(msm)),
    ipwvcov = sqrt(ipwvcov(w_ipw[[est]], msm)[1, 1]),
    coxph_weightit.asympt = sqrt(vcov(fit_w)[1, 1]),
    robust.coxph = sqrt(msm$var[1, 1]))
}))
round(cox_table, 4)
#>      log.hr ipwvcov coxph_weightit.asympt robust.coxph
#> ATE -0.4718  0.0833                0.0835       0.0941
#> ATT -0.4120  0.0826                0.0832       0.0884
#> ATC -0.5458  0.1058                0.1105       0.1145
#> ATO -0.4637  0.0844                0.0844       0.0896

ipwvcov() uses the weighted partial likelihood score as the estimating equation and accounts for the weights in both each person’s own term and the risk-set sums; the package tests check it against central finite differences of the stacked estimating equations (agreement about 1e-7). WeightIt’s values are close but not identical: its vcov = "HC0" equals coxph()’s robust variance exactly, so the difference lies in how the estimated weights enter. In our checks the relative difference was below 0.1% for ATE and overlap weights and shrank with the sample size; for ATT and ATC weights WeightIt’s standard error was 1 to 4% larger and the difference did not shrink (ATC in the table above). ipwvcov() equals the finite-difference reference on these data too. The methods article gives details.

The table below summarises a simulation (500 people per data set, treatment depending on a confounder, conditional hazard ratio exp(-0.5), administrative censoring) of 95% Wald intervals for the marginal log hazard ratio. The truth is the marginal log hazard ratio in the target population, computed from both potential outcomes of a very large sample. The bootstrap (200 samples, weights re-estimated in each) was run on a subset of the data sets.

knitr::kable(cox_sim$summary, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
estimand truth mean.estimate empirical.sd mean.se.ipwvcov mean.se.robust mean.se.bootstrap coverage.ipwvcov coverage.robust coverage.bootstrap replications bootstrap.replications
ATE -0.450 -0.447 0.128 0.128 0.14 0.128 0.956 0.969 0.95 1000 300
ATO -0.461 -0.460 0.133 0.132 0.14 0.133 0.956 0.961 0.95 1000 300

The mean ipwvcov() standard error is within 1% of the empirical standard deviation of the estimates for both estimands, and so is the bootstrap’s. The robust standard error, which treats the weights as known, is about 10% (ATE) and 6% (ATO) too large here, so its intervals cover more often than 95%: conservative, but wider than needed. The coverages of ipwvcov() (1000 data sets) and of the bootstrap (300 data sets) are both within simulation error of 95%.

ipwvcov() covers binary exposures with logistic exposure models: point treatments with lm(), glm() or coxph() outcome models, and time-varying weights from ipwtm() (section 3). WeightIt’s outcome-model functions cover more: multi-category and continuous treatments, many weighting methods, and ordinal and multinomial outcome models.

2. Categorical point treatment

A treatment with three levels, A, B and C. With estimand = "ATT" and a focal level, people at that level keep weight 1 and the others are reweighted to resemble them; estimand = "ATO" gives generalized overlap weights (Li & Li 2019).

set.seed(31)
n <- 1000
dc <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n), z = rnorm(n))
pr <- cbind(1, exp(0.5 + 0.8 * dc$l), exp(-0.3 - 0.6 * dc$l + 0.4 * dc$z))
pr <- pr / rowSums(pr)
dc$m <- factor(apply(pr, 1, function(p) sample(c("A", "B", "C"), 1, prob = p)))
table(dc$m)
#> 
#>   A   B   C 
#> 251 510 239
compare <- function(estimand, focal = NULL, ...) {
  wi <- ipwpoint(exposure = m, family = "multinomial", denominator = ~ l + z, data = dc,
                 estimand = estimand, focal = focal, ...)$ipw.weights
  ww <- WeightIt::weightit(m ~ l + z, data = dc, method = "glm",
                           estimand = estimand, focal = focal)$weights
  max(abs(wi / ww - 1))
}
rbind(
  default.multinom = c(ATT.focal.A = compare("ATT", "A"), ATO = compare("ATO")),
  tight.multinom = c(ATT.focal.A = compare("ATT", "A", reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000),
                     ATO = compare("ATO", reltol = 1e-12, maxit = 1000)))
#>                   ATT.focal.A          ATO
#> default.multinom 6.282293e-04 9.086836e-04
#> tight.multinom   2.844251e-08 3.185674e-08

The table shows the largest relative difference between the weights. ipw fits the multinomial model with nnet::multinom(), which by default stops when the relative change in the fit criterion falls below 1e-8; that leaves relative differences of up to about 1e-3 from WeightIt, whose own fitter converges further. With a tighter tolerance (reltol, passed on through ...), the weights agree to about 1e-8: the formulas are the same.

PSweight fits the multinomial model with the same defaults as nnet::multinom(), so its weights (scaled to sum to 1 within each level) agree with ipw’s default fit to rounding error; its trtgrp is ipw’s focal:

compare_psw <- function(estimand, weight, focal = NULL) {
  wi <- ipwpoint(exposure = m, family = "multinomial", denominator = ~ l + z, data = dc,
                 estimand = estimand, focal = focal)$ipw.weights
  wp <- PSweight::SumStat(ps.formula = m ~ l + z, data = dc, weight = weight,
                          trtgrp = focal)$ps.weights[[weight]]
  max(abs(wi / ave(wi, dc$m, FUN = sum) / (wp / ave(wp, dc$m, FUN = sum)) - 1))
}
c(ATE = compare_psw("ATE", "IPW"), ATT.focal.A = compare_psw("ATT", "treated", "A"),
  ATO = compare_psw("ATO", "overlap"))
#>          ATE  ATT.focal.A          ATO 
#> 0.000000e+00 0.000000e+00 2.220446e-16

Within each level, the ATT weights make the covariate means resemble those of the focal group:

w_att <- ipwpoint(exposure = m, family = "multinomial", denominator = ~ l + z,
                  data = dc, estimand = "ATT", focal = "A")$ipw.weights
rbind(unweighted = tapply(dc$l, dc$m, mean),
      ATT.focal.A = sapply(levels(dc$m), function(k)
        weighted.mean(dc$l[dc$m == k], w_att[dc$m == k])))
#>                      A          B          C
#> unweighted  -0.2166951  0.4582985 -0.6187572
#> ATT.focal.A -0.2166951 -0.2541368 -0.2024986

For an ordered exposure, ipw uses MASS::polr() (family = "ordinal"); WeightIt also fits an ordinal model for an ordered factor. In the package tests the two agree to 1e-4 or better.

3. Longitudinal data with individual visit times

Here the two packages are designed differently.

  • ipwtm() works on long data: one row per person per interval between visits, with tstart and timevar. The exposure model is fitted once, pooled over all rows (a Cox model, a pooled logistic regression, or a multinomial, ordinal or GEE model), so each person can have their own number of visits at their own times.
  • weightitMSM() works on wide data: one row per person, and one treatment model per time point, given in formula.list. Its help page states that only wide data are supported. The time points are therefore the same for everyone. The weight is the product of the weights at the time points. This fits designs with fixed visits, such as yearly measurements in a cohort or a trial with scheduled visits, and it allows any WeightIt method at each time point.

Data with individual visit times

We simulate 1000 people followed for 5 years. Each person is seen at their own times, about twice a year on average with random gaps. At each visit a confounder l is measured; it depends on its previous value and on treatment. People not yet treated may start treatment at a visit, more likely when l is low. Once started, treatment continues.

set.seed(11)
n <- 1000
sim_person <- function(i) {
  t <- 0; l <- rnorm(1); a <- 0; l0 <- l; rows <- list()
  repeat {
    t_next <- t + rexp(1, rate = 2)           # gap to the next visit
    if (t_next > 5) break
    l <- 0.8 * l + 0.4 * a + rnorm(1, 0, 0.5)  # confounder measured at the visit
    start <- if (a == 0) rbinom(1, 1, plogis(-2.5 - 1.0 * l)) else 0
    rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(id = i, tstart = t, time = t_next,
                                           l0 = l0, l = l, start = start)
    if (start == 1) a <- 1
    t <- t_next
  }
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n), sim_person))
long$a <- ave(long$start, long$id, FUN = cummax)   # 1 from the visit of starting on
head(long[, c("id", "tstart", "time", "l", "a")], 4)
#>   id     tstart       time           l a
#> 1  1 0.00000000 0.01060837 -1.57079786 1
#> 2  1 0.01060837 1.24229627 -1.13336715 1
#> 3  1 1.24229627 2.34270656  0.01376242 1
#> 4  1 2.34270656 2.41639228  0.38814845 1
c(people = n, rows = nrow(long), started = sum(long$start))
#>  people    rows started 
#>    1000   10040     576
summary(as.vector(table(long$id)))   # number of visits per person
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    2.00    8.00   10.00   10.04   12.00   22.00

ipw: the long data as they are

ipwtm() fits a Cox model for the time to starting treatment on the intervals between each person’s own visits; with type = "first" the rows after the start are not used for the model and keep the weight reached at the start.

w_tm <- ipwtm(exposure = a, family = "survival", numerator = ~ l0,
              denominator = ~ l0 + l, id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = time,
              type = "first", data = long)
summary(w_tm$ipw.weights)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.1936  0.8119  0.9513  0.9980  1.0614  5.2554

The weights can be used directly in a weighted model on the same rows, for example coxph(Surv(tstart, time, event) ~ a + l0, weights = w_tm$ipw.weights, ...) for an outcome event.

WeightIt: a common time grid first

For weightitMSM(), the data must first be put on time points that are the same for everyone, say the end of each year. At each time point k, the analyst has to choose a value of l and of the treatment. A common choice is the last value observed up to k (the baseline value if there was no visit yet) and “started by k”:

grid <- 1:5
last_before <- function(k, column, default) {
  sub <- long[long$time <= k, ]
  last <- sub[!duplicated(sub$id, fromLast = TRUE), ]   # rows are in time order
  out <- default
  out[last$id] <- last[[column]]
  out
}
l0 <- long$l0[!duplicated(long$id)]
wide <- data.frame(id = seq_len(n), l0 = l0)
for (k in grid) {
  wide[[paste0("L", k)]] <- last_before(k, "l", l0)
  wide[[paste0("A", k)]] <- last_before(k, "a", rep(0, n))
}
head(wide, 3)
#>   id         l0          L1 A1         L2 A2         L3 A3         L4 A4
#> 1  1 -0.5910311 -1.57079786  1 -1.1333671  1  0.3881485  1  0.7743123  1
#> 2  2  0.8877716  0.07944407  0 -0.1577471  0 -0.1577471  0 -0.4809450  0
#> 3  3 -1.5774979 -1.10960567  0 -1.2076286  0 -0.7749272  0 -0.8303085  0
#>           L5 A5
#> 1  0.5324167  1
#> 2 -1.1703153  0
#> 3 -0.9115556  0

One model per time point, each with the treatment history and the confounder history up to then (here the previous treatment and current l), and a numerator model with the treatment history and baseline l0:

formulas <- lapply(grid, function(k)
  as.formula(if (k == 1) "A1 ~ l0 + L1" else
               sprintf("A%d ~ A%d + l0 + L%d", k, k - 1, k)))
num_formulas <- lapply(grid, function(k)
  as.formula(if (k == 1) "~ l0" else sprintf("~ A%d + l0", k - 1)))
w_msm <- WeightIt::weightitMSM(formulas, data = wide, method = "glm",
                               stabilize = TRUE, num.formula = num_formulas)
summary(w_msm$weights)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.4485  0.9055  0.9797  1.0053  1.0731  2.5403

glm() warns here (warnings hidden) that fitted probabilities of 0 or 1 occurred: people who already started have A(k-1) = 1 and therefore A(k) = 1, so the model at each time point also “predicts” a treatment that is no longer a choice; their factor is about 1. This matches what type = "first" does in ipw by leaving those rows out of the model.

What the grid means for such data

The grid analysis uses the data in a coarser form. How much is lost depends on how far the visit times are from the grid:

starts <- long[long$start == 1, ]
grid_k <- ceiling(starts$time)                     # grid point at which the start is seen
l_at_grid <- mapply(function(i, k) wide[i, paste0("L", k)], starts$id, grid_k)
last_visit <- sapply(grid, function(k) {
  sub <- long[long$time <= k, ]
  mean(k - tapply(sub$time, sub$id, max))
})
c(visits.per.person = nrow(long) / n,
  grid.points.per.person = length(grid),
  starts.l.differs.from.l.at.start = mean(abs(l_at_grid - starts$l) > 1e-12),
  mean.years.between.last.visit.and.grid.point = mean(last_visit))
#>                            visits.per.person 
#>                                   10.0400000 
#>                       grid.points.per.person 
#>                                    5.0000000 
#>             starts.l.differs.from.l.at.start 
#>                                    0.5677083 
#> mean.years.between.last.visit.and.grid.point 
#>                                    0.4598103
  • Timing. About ten visits per person are reduced to five time points. A start at 1.1 and one at 1.9 years are both “started by year 2”.
  • Which l. For more than half of the people who started, the l used at the grid point is not the value measured at the visit where treatment was started. It comes from a later visit in the same year, measured after the start and so possibly affected by treatment, which the treatment model should not adjust for. Using the value at the start instead needs extra data preparation.
  • Carried-forward values. On average the last visit was about half a year before the grid point, so for people who did not start, l is older than the time point it stands for.

A finer grid (for example monthly) reduces these problems, but means many more time points with few or no visits, each with its own model and many carried-forward values. Neither the grid analysis nor the long-data analysis is wrong in general: with scheduled visits that everyone attends, the grid is the design, and weightitMSM() offers the full range of WeightIt methods at each time point. With visit times that differ between people, ipwtm() uses each person’s own intervals directly.

Standard errors on long data

With pooled logistic models (ipwtm(family = "binomial", link = "logit"), any type), ipwvcov() gives M-estimation standard errors for an MSM fitted on the long data with lm(), glm() or a Cox model on counting-process data, summing all scores within each person; a list of weight objects, such as treatment and censoring weights, can be passed. For the Cox exposure models used above (family = "survival") it is not available, and the cluster bootstrap remains the option.

When the visits are at the same times for everyone, the two packages can be compared exactly: with time-specific columns in the pooled model the weights equal those of weightitMSM(), and the package tests show that ipwvcov() then reproduces glm_weightit(vcov = "asympt") for a person-level outcome to about 1e-6.

The table summarises a simulation with individual visit times (300 people with 3 to 7 visits; a confounder that changes over time; a treatment that switches back and forth and depends on the confounder and on the previous treatment; an outcome at every visit with an effect of current treatment of 1). In the “moderate” scenario treatment depends moderately on the confounder and on the previous treatment; in the “strong” scenario twice as strongly, which gives cumulative weights with a heavy right tail (see the median of the largest weight). The weights are ipwtm(type = "all", numerator = ~ blag, denominator = ~ blag + l) and the MSM is lm(y ~ b) on all rows. The robust standard error is clustered by person (HC0) and treats the weights as known; the cluster bootstrap (200 samples of persons, weights re-estimated in each) was run on a subset of the data sets.

knitr::kable(tm_sim$summary, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
scenario median.max.weight mean.estimate empirical.sd mean.se.ipwvcov mean.se.robust mean.se.bootstrap coverage.ipwvcov coverage.robust coverage.bootstrap replications bootstrap.replications
moderate 4.152 1.001 0.057 0.059 0.082 0.058 0.958 0.990 0.965 1000 200
strong 12.013 1.006 0.101 0.084 0.109 0.084 0.930 0.973 0.945 1000 200

With moderate weights, ipwvcov() and the cluster bootstrap agree with each other and with the empirical standard deviation of the estimates, and their intervals cover about 95%. The robust standard error, which treats the weights as known, is about 40% too large here, so its intervals are much wider than needed. With strongly dependent treatment, ipwvcov() and the bootstrap give almost the same standard error, but both are about 17% smaller than the empirical standard deviation, and coverage drops to about 93% (the bootstrap’s 94.5% is based on 200 data sets). The robust standard error is conservative in both scenarios here, but that is not guaranteed; the package’s simulation study found settings where it was too small as well.

Heavy-tailed weights

Why do both methods fall short in the strong scenario? Cumulative weights are products of many factors. When some people have a very low probability of their observed treatment history (a near-violation of positivity), the weights have a heavy right tail: P(W > x) falls off like x−γx^{-\gamma} for a tail index γ\gamma. The weights have a finite variance only if γ>2\gamma > 2. The normal approximation also relies on a finite third moment (γ>3\gamma > 3), and estimating the variance well, by the sandwich or by the bootstrap, relies on a finite fourth moment (γ>4\gamma > 4).

To check this explanation, the strong scenario and a milder version of it (dependence on the confounder and on the previous treatment three quarters as strong) were run with 300, 1200 and 4800 people. The weight distribution refers to the final cumulative weight of each person: the largest weight and the 99.9th percentile (medians over data sets), the Kish effective sample size as a fraction of n (mean), and the Hill estimate of the tail index from the top 5% (median). There were 1000, 1000 and 500 data sets per size, of which 200, 200 and 100 were bootstrapped (B = 200).

tail_tab <- tm_tail$summary[, c("scenario", "n", "max.weight", "q999.weight",
                                "ess.fraction", "hill.tail.index",
                                "empirical.sd", "mean.se.ipwvcov",
                                "mean.se.bootstrap", "coverage.ipwvcov",
                                "coverage.bootstrap", "coverage.robust")]
knitr::kable(tail_tab, digits = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 3, 3, 3), row.names = FALSE)
scenario n max.weight q999.weight ess.fraction hill.tail.index empirical.sd mean.se.ipwvcov mean.se.bootstrap coverage.ipwvcov coverage.bootstrap coverage.robust

strong 1200 17.2 11.5 0.44 2.29 0.0499 0.0453 0.0440 0.932 0.945 0.975
strong 4800 33.1 13.2 0.39 2.26 0.0290 0.0257 0.0264 0.918 0.900 0.980
milder 300 6.6 6.2 0.63 2.87 0.0747 0.0691 0.0688 0.939 0.935 0.983
milder 1200 10.7 7.6 0.61 2.83 0.0404 0.0367 0.0358 0.934 0.945 0.987
milder 4800 18.0 8.5 0.60 2.81 0.0203 0.0188 0.0192 0.946 0.930 0.996

The Hill estimate from one sample of 200,000 people per scenario, at three tail fractions, with the largest weight and the effective sample size fraction in that sample (“moderate” is the moderate scenario above):

knitr::kable(tm_tail$hill_big, digits = 2)
strong milder moderate
hill_5pct 2.28 2.76 3.90
hill_1pct 2.35 2.82 3.76
hill_0.2pct 2.33 2.66 3.45
max.weight 144.66 58.92 24.48
ess.fraction 0.40 0.59 0.80

The tail index is above 2 in every scenario, so the weights have a finite variance and the intervals are valid in the limit. It is, however, about 2.3 in the strong scenario and 2.8 in the milder one, compared with 3.9 in the moderate scenario. Coverage of ipwvcov() intervals follows the tail index: about 95% (moderate), about 94% (milder) and 92 to 93% (strong). In the strong scenario coverage does not improve from 300 to 4800 people, while the largest weight roughly doubles with every fourfold increase in n and the effective sample size fraction keeps falling. The cluster bootstrap gives about the same standard errors as ipwvcov() and does no better (its coverage rests on 100 to 200 data sets, so it is uncertain by about 2 to 3 percentage points).

Heavy-tailed weights therefore make normal-theory intervals unreliable for any method, the bootstrap included. The variance formula is not the cause: it matches the numerical Jacobian of the estimating equations exactly. Check the weight distribution (summary(), ipwplot(), the effective sample size) before trusting any standard error. If a few people carry much of the weight, consider truncation, a less extreme weight model or a different estimand.

4. Which to use

  • WeightIt for point treatments when you want machine-learning or balancing methods (GBM, SuperLearner, BART, CBPS, entropy balancing, energy balancing, …), many estimands, balance diagnostics through cobalt and M-estimation standard errors for outcome models (glm_weightit(), coxph_weightit(), …). Also for longitudinal treatments measured at fixed time points that are the same for everyone.
  • ipw for exposures that change over time in long (counting-process) data with each person’s own visit times; Cox models for the time to the first switch or to censoring (ipwtm(family = "survival")); exposures that switch back and forth or recur (type = "all"); count and skewed continuous exposures (Poisson, negative binomial, gamma, log-normal); and analyses with few dependencies. With pooled logistic exposure models, ipwvcov() gives M-estimation standard errors on the long data.
  • PSweight for point treatments when you want overlap, matching or entropy weights with built-in sandwich standard errors, augmented (doubly robust) estimators, ratio estimands for binary outcomes, or survey or clustered data.
  • For a binary or categorical point treatment with a logistic model, the three give the same weights; for a binary one, ipwvcov(), glm_weightit(vcov = "asympt") and PSweight give the same standard errors.

The README has a comparison table.
